Glaze could be brushed on, or form from a glazing powder in which an object was buried.

Lead crystal is glass made heavy and brilliant with lead oxide. In 1674 George Ravenscroft patented a clear English glass meant to rival rock crystal; when early pieces clouded, a defect called crizzling, he added lead, a change dated between 1674 and 1676. The denser, more refractive glass suited cut tableware and, later, the flint elements of achromatic lenses.

Gliding flight depends on wings that generate lift and on controls that keep the craft balanced. George Cayley analysed lift, drag and thrust and flew a crewed glider at Brompton Dale in 1853. Otto Lilienthal made about 2,000 glides in 1891-1896 and published lift data. The Wright brothers' gliders of 1900-1902 developed control around three axes.

Gold, which does not tarnish, and more rarely silver occur as soft native metal that can be worked without smelting. The cemetery at Varna, Bulgaria, used around 4600-4200 BCE, held more than 3,000 gold objects weighing about six kilograms, the oldest large assemblage of worked gold known. How far that wealth reflects a ranked society is debated.

Satellite navigation fixes position by timing radio signals from several satellites that carry atomic clocks. The United States Global Positioning System, developed from 1973, reached full operational capability in 1995. Its clocks are corrected for special and general relativity, about 38 microseconds a day; uncorrected, fixes would drift by kilometres daily. Civil receivers spread widely during the 1990s.

Graphics processors were built to compute colours for millions of screen pixels at once, using many simple cores working in parallel. Chips marketed as GPUs appeared in 1999, and from 2006-07 programming tools such as NVIDIA's CUDA let scientists use them for general calculations. They suited simulation and matrix arithmetic, later the core workload of machine learning.

Graphite-moderated reactors use very pure carbon to slow neutrons, letting unenriched uranium sustain a chain reaction. Oak Ridge's X-10 (1943) pioneered plutonium production that Hanford's B reactor (1944) took to full scale. Britain's Magnox stations, from Calder Hall in 1956, cooled such cores with carbon dioxide for power. Flaws in the Soviet RBMK variant contributed to Chernobyl in 1986.

Greek fire was a liquid incendiary used by the Byzantine navy, projected from pressurised siphons in the bows of ships. Byzantine tradition credits a refugee architect from Syria named Kallinikos, with its first use during the Arab sieges of Constantinople around 672–678. The composition was a closely guarded state secret, probably petroleum-based, and its formula was later lost.

From the 1940s Norman Borlaug, working in Mexico, bred short-stemmed wheat that could take heavy fertilizer without toppling; in 1966 the International Rice Research Institute released IR8, a semi-dwarf rice. With irrigation, fertilizer and pesticides, these varieties sharply raised yields in India, Pakistan and elsewhere. Critics note uneven gains favouring irrigated, better-off farmers, and environmental costs.

Grid-scale storage holds surplus electricity and returns it when demand peaks or wind and sunlight fall away. The oldest method is pumped storage: water is pumped uphill and later released through turbines, used in Switzerland and Italy from the late nineteenth century. It still holds most installed storage capacity, while large battery installations multiplied in the 2010s.

Grinding wild seeds and roots between two stones turns tough plant tissue into flour or paste that cooks quickly. Starch grains on grinding tools from Bilancino in Italy, Kostenki in Russia and Pavlov in Czechia show mobile hunter-gatherers processing plants this way about 30,000 years ago. Later, Natufian foragers of the Levant pounded wild cereals in stone mortars.

Grinding a stone blade against an abrasive rock produces a smooth, strong edge that can be resharpened by further grinding, suited to felling and heavy woodworking. A ground-edge axe fragment from Carpenter's Gap 1 in Western Australia's Kimberley is dated to 44,000-49,000 years ago; Japan has ground-edge axes about 35,000-38,000 years old, long before farming.

Guided missiles combine propulsion with a guidance system that corrects their course in flight. Germany's Henschel Hs 293, a rocket-boosted glide bomb steered by radio, was first used in August 1943 and soon sank Allied ships, including HMS Egret. In the 1950s homing missiles entered service, such as the American infrared-guided Sidewinder, adopted by the US Navy in 1956.

Precision-guided munitions steer onto a marked or located target. American laser-guided bombs, homing on laser light reflected from the target, destroyed the Thanh Hoa bridge in North Vietnam in 1972 after years of failed raids with unguided bombs. From the 1990s, bombs guided by satellite navigation could strike set coordinates in any weather. Misidentified targets still cause civilian deaths.

Gunpowder mixes saltpetre (potassium nitrate), sulphur and charcoal; the saltpetre supplies oxygen, so the mixture burns fiercely without air. Chinese alchemists searching for elixirs came upon such mixtures by the ninth century. The Wujing Zongyao, compiled about 1040-1044, holds the earliest surviving military formulas, which were low in saltpetre and made incendiaries rather than explosives.

Plants need fixed nitrogen, yet the nitrogen in air is unreactive. By 1908 Fritz Haber showed that high pressure and a catalyst could make ammonia directly from nitrogen and hydrogen. Carl Bosch's team at BASF, running thousands of catalyst trials, scaled it up, and the Oppau plant began production in 1913. Its ammonia supplied fertiliser and, in wartime, explosives.

Before coins, silver served as money by weight. Mesopotamian texts state prices and debts in shekels, a weight unit of about 8.4 grams. Payers cut rings, coils and ingots into pieces, now called hacksilver, and weighed them on balances. The silver itself was refined from lead-bearing ores by cupellation, attested from the fourth millennium BCE.

Composite hafting joins a stone tip or blade to a shaft or handle with a shaped tang or socket, binding and glue, to survive repeated impact. Damage on points from Kathu Pan 1, South Africa, about 500,000 years old, has been read as hafted spear tips, a contested claim; glued hafts are secure by about 70,000 years ago.

Controlled heating of silcrete or chert alters the stone so that it fractures more smoothly; heated pieces leave glossy rather than dull flake scars. Evidence from Pinnacle Point, South Africa, points to the practice by about 164,000 years ago, and experiments showed unheated Blombos silcrete could hardly be pressure-flaked. It is an early case of fire altering a material.

The heavy plough combined a coulter, an iron share and a mouldboard, and might need up to eight oxen. It turned the wet clay soils of northern Europe that resisted the ard. Linguistic evidence suggests Slavic peoples used it by the sixth century CE, and it is recorded in Italy's Po valley by 643; how fast it spread is debated.

Heavy water, whose hydrogen carries an extra neutron, absorbs so few neutrons that a reactor moderated by it can run on natural uranium. Canada's ZEEP at Chalk River, critical in September 1945, was the first reactor outside the United States. The CANDU design, from a 1962 prototype, holds fuel in pressure tubes and refuels while running. India also uses it.

A helicopter lifts and steers itself with powered rotating wings, so it can hover, take off vertically and land without runways. Rotor torque and uneven blade forces defeated many early attempts. In 1935 and 1936 France's Breguet-Dorand Gyroplane Laboratoire and Germany's Focke-Wulf Fw 61 made controlled flights; Igor Sikorsky's VS-300 (1939) then established the single main rotor with tail rotor.

Nicolaus Copernicus's On the Revolutions (1543) placed the Sun at the centre and treated Earth as one of the planets, though he kept circular orbits. Using Tycho Brahe's careful observations, Johannes Kepler showed in Astronomia nova (1609) that Mars moves on an ellipse and sweeps equal areas in equal times. The Sun-centred system remained contested for decades.

Hereditary rank exists when status and leadership pass by descent within particular families, so control of land, herds and surplus is inherited rather than won anew each generation. Archaeologists infer it from burials: at Varna in Bulgaria, graves of about 4600-4200 BCE range from plain pits to a few rich in gold. Whether such wealth was inherited is debated.

Hide working turns raw skins into durable leather or fur by scraping away flesh and fat, then drying, stretching and softening them, sometimes with fat or smoke. Stone scrapers with hide-use wear, and specialised bone tools in Africa and Europe, show the practice by at least 100,000 years ago. Hides gave clothing, containers and tent covers.

Egyptian hieroglyphic writing combined signs for words with signs for consonant sounds. Inscribed labels from tomb U-j at Abydos, dated to around 3250 BCE, are among its earliest known examples. Whether Egypt invented writing independently or after contact with Mesopotamia is debated. Hieroglyphs served monuments and ritual for over three millennia, while cursive hieratic handled daily administration.

High-speed rail runs passenger trains at sustained speeds above roughly 200 kilometres per hour on dedicated, carefully engineered track. Japan opened the Tokaido Shinkansen between Tokyo and Shin-Osaka in October 1964, using electric multiple-unit trains, gentle curves, tunnels and viaducts. France followed with the TGV in 1981. Over medium distances, such lines often rival air travel on door-to-door journey time.

Indian mathematicians developed decimal place-value numerals with a sign for zero by the mid-first millennium CE, and in 628 Brahmagupta set out rules for calculating with zero and negative numbers. Al-Khwarizmi's treatise on Indian reckoning, written in Baghdad around 820, spread the system westward, and Fibonacci's Liber Abaci of 1202 promoted it in a Europe still using Roman numerals.

The horizontal treadle loom lets the weaver's feet raise and lower sets of warp threads through cords and levers, freeing both hands to pass the shuttle and beat in the weft. Loom models from a Han-dynasty tomb at Laoguanshan, Chengdu, date to about 150 BCE. In Europe, eleventh-century loom parts mark its arrival as the professional weaver's tool.

The oral contraceptive uses synthetic hormones resembling progesterone to stop ovulation. It joined reproductive endocrinology to steroid chemistry: Russell Marker's route from Mexican wild yams made steroids cheap, and norethindrone was synthesised in Mexico City in 1951. Gregory Pincus, John Rock and colleagues ran clinical trials, and a pill was first approved for contraception in the United States in 1960.

A padded collar rests on a horse's shoulders, letting it pull heavy loads with its full strength instead of against straps across its chest or neck. Collar harness is attested in China by about the fifth century CE and became widespread in Europe around the tenth to twelfth centuries. Horses could then plough and haul faster than oxen.

Horse husbandry began on the Eurasian steppes. At Botai, Kazakhstan, people depended heavily on horses by about 3500 BCE, though whether those animals were domestic is disputed; genomes show they were not ancestors of today's horses. The modern domestic lineage emerged near the lower Don and Volga and spread across much of western Eurasia from about 2200 BCE.

A nailed horseshoe is an iron rim fixed to the hoof wall with nails, protecting hooves worn by hard roads, stony ground or wet conditions. Romans used strap-on hipposandals; nailed shoes were common in Europe by about the 10th century CE, though the date of the first ones is contested. Shod horses could keep working on paved and muddy surfaces.

Hot blast means preheating the air blown into a blast furnace. James Beaumont Neilson, manager of the Glasgow gas works, patented the idea in 1828. Heating the air to about 300 degrees Fahrenheit cut coal per ton of iron by over a third in one reported case, allowed raw coal instead of coke, and made Scotland's blackband ironstone worth smelting.

A hydroelectric station drops water from a dam or diverted river through turbines that drive generators. The Adams station at Niagara Falls, opened in 1895, was a landmark: from 1896 it sent three-phase alternating current to Buffalo. Large dams later gave cheap continuous power to energy-hungry industries such as aluminium smelting, whose electrolytic process dates from 1886.

An intercontinental ballistic missile is a rocket that carries a warhead thousands of kilometres, mostly above the atmosphere, before re-entering at very high speed. The Soviet R-7 made the first successful long-range flight in August 1957 and soon afterwards launched Sputnik. Usually armed with thermonuclear warheads, ICBMs became central to Cold War deterrence and to later arms-control treaties.

Immunology studies the body's defences against infection. In Berlin in 1890, Emil von Behring and Kitasato Shibasaburō showed that immunised animals produced blood antitoxins against diphtheria or tetanus toxins, and that such serum could protect others, founding serum therapy. In 1901 Karl Landsteiner used the clumping of red cells by serum to define blood groups, later central to transfusion.

Variolation protected against smallpox by deliberately infecting a healthy person with material from a smallpox sore or scab, usually producing a milder illness and lasting immunity. It was practised in China, where powdered scabs were blown into the nose, and in India, the Ottoman world and West Africa before reaching Britain in 1721. Recipients could still die or infect others.

An integrated circuit forms transistors, resistors and their connections together on one piece of semiconductor instead of wiring separate parts. Jack Kilby at Texas Instruments demonstrated one in 1958, and Robert Noyce at Fairchild devised a planar silicon version in 1959, independently. Patterning by photolithography, related to photographic printing, let factories make many identical chips together.

Interchangeable manufacture makes each part so close to a master pattern, shaped with jigs and machine tools and checked with gauges, that it fits without hand filing. Honoré Blanc demonstrated interchangeable musket locks in France in the 1780s. In the 1820s John Hall made interchangeable rifle parts at Harpers Ferry Armory, a basis of the American system of manufactures.

A high-speed petrol engine burns a volatile liquid fuel inside its cylinders and turns much faster than stationary gas engines, giving more power for its weight. Gottlieb Daimler and Wilhelm Maybach at Cannstatt (1883-84) and Karl Benz at Mannheim (1885) developed such engines independently. They ran on light petroleum spirit: in 1888 Bertha Benz bought some at a Wiesloch pharmacy.

The internet links separate computer networks through shared rules for sending data in addressed packets. ARPANET, funded by the US Defense Department, connected its first nodes in 1969. Vinton Cerf and Robert Kahn designed TCP/IP, adopted across ARPANET on 1 January 1983. Tim Berners-Lee's World Wide Web, released from CERN in 1991, made linked documents widely accessible.

A bloomery reduces iron ore with charcoal in a furnace without melting the metal, yielding a spongy bloom of iron and slag that smiths consolidate by repeated hammering. Unlike tin, iron ores are widespread. Systematic bloomery production spread from about 1200 BCE in Anatolia and nearby regions; Central African furnaces are dated to the ninth century BCE.

Iron hulls freed ship size from the limits of timber by riveting wrought-iron plates over iron frames. The paddle steamer Aaron Manby, built in 1821, became the first iron steamship to go to sea in 1822. Brunel's SS Great Britain, launched in 1843, combined an iron hull with screw propulsion and was the largest ship afloat at the time.

A mouldboard is a curved plate behind the ploughshare that lifts and turns the cut soil, burying weeds and stubble instead of merely scratching a furrow. In China iron mouldboard ploughs were probably developed by the fourth century BCE and were common under the Han dynasty (206 BCE to 220 CE), alongside other iron farm tools.

Basin irrigation encloses floodplain fields with earth banks so a river's seasonal flood can be let in, held for weeks to soak the soil and leave silt, then drained before sowing. In Egypt it grew from simpler flood-recession farming over the fourth and third millennia BCE. It gave one dependable crop a year, though failed floods still brought hunger.

Canal irrigation leads river water through dug channels to fields beyond the reach of rain or flood. At Choga Mami in eastern Iraq, Samarran-period canals date to about 6,000 BCE. Comparable systems arose independently in the Andes and the American Southwest. Over centuries, evaporation from poorly drained fields can leave salt behind, as documented in southern Mesopotamia.

In-vitro fertilisation joins egg and sperm outside the body and returns the resulting embryo to the uterus. It rests on reproductive endocrinology, which allows ovulation to be timed or stimulated, and on embryo culture. Louise Brown, the first child born after IVF, was born in England in 1978 after work by Robert Edwards and Patrick Steptoe, using a natural cycle.

A Jacquard head selects which warp threads rise for each weft pass from a chain of punched cards: where a card has a hole, the linked hook lifts its thread. It automated the drawloom's figure harness, worked by an assistant, the drawboy. Joseph-Marie Jacquard developed it in Lyon about 1804, building on earlier devices by Bouchon (1725), Falcon (1728) and Vaucanson (1745).

Jet airliners carry passengers on gas-turbine engines, cruising higher and faster than piston aircraft. Britain's de Havilland Comet began scheduled service in 1952, but fatal crashes later traced to metal fatigue grounded it in 1954. Boeing's 707, entering service in 1958, helped make long-haul jet travel commercially viable. Turbine blades of creep-resistant nickel alloys kept such engines dependable.

A turbojet draws in air, compresses it, burns fuel in it and expands the hot gas through a turbine that drives the compressor; the remaining exhaust pushes the aircraft forward. Frank Whittle in Britain and Hans von Ohain in Germany developed the idea independently in the 1930s. Von Ohain's engine flew in August 1939, Whittle's in 1941.

A joint-stock company divides its capital into transferable shares held by many investors and has a legal identity and management separate from its owners, letting it pool large sums for long, risky ventures. England's East India Company (1600) and the Dutch East India Company (1602), whose shares traded in Amsterdam, were influential early examples, building on older partnership forms.

An updraft kiln separates fire from pots: fuel burns in a lower chamber and hot gases rise through a perforated floor into the ware above. Enclosure allows higher, steadier temperatures and some control of the atmosphere. In northern Mesopotamia simple pit kilns appear in the early sixth millennium BCE and two-chamber kilns by its middle, in the Halaf period.

A council of elders brings together the heads of households or lineages to settle quarrels, share out common land, water or hunting grounds, and agree on joint action. Its authority rests on age, kinship and persuasion rather than force. Ethnographers have recorded such councils among many foraging and farming peoples; their prehistoric antiquity is inferred, not dated.

Blades are long, narrow, parallel-sided flakes struck in series from a carefully maintained core. Blade and bladelet production from prismatic cores is documented in southern Africa's Howiesons Poort, roughly 65,000 years ago, and blade industries spread across Eurasia from about 45,000 years ago, as at Bacho Kiro, Bulgaria. One core could supply blanks for many tool forms.

In the Levallois method a knapper first shapes a stone core so that one blow detaches a flake of planned size and outline. The approach grew from simpler prepared-core methods and became widespread in Africa and western Eurasia around 300,000 years ago; in southwestern China it appears between about 170,000 and 80,000 years ago.

Knapping strikes one stone against another to detach sharp-edged flakes. Oldowan tools, named after Olduvai Gorge, Tanzania, appear at Gona, Ethiopia, by about 2.6 million years ago. At Nyayanga, Kenya, they lie among cut-marked hippopotamus bones, with wear from processing animals and plants. Cruder Lomekwian pieces from Kenya, about 3.3 million years old, remain debated.

Lacquer is the sap of the lacquer tree, brushed on in thin coats that harden through slow chemical curing into a waterproof, durable and glossy film. A red-lacquered wooden bowl from Hemudu, Zhejiang, long held as earliest, dates to roughly the fifth millennium BCE; lacquered wood from nearby Jingtoushan is reported as more than 8,000 years old.

A lamp makes fire portable and steady: a hollowed stone holds animal fat that burns on a wick of plant fibre. Stone lamps are known from Upper Palaeolithic sites in France, among them a carved sandstone lamp from Lascaux, a cave painted roughly 17,000 years ago. Lamps gave a small, steady light for working in deep caves.

A land registry is a public record, kept by officials, of each plot's boundaries, holder and dues; it is evidence of title and the basis of assessment. Egyptian scribes surveyed fields for assessment from the third millennium BCE; England's Domesday survey of 1086 recorded landholdings; and Robert Torrens's system of registered title began in South Australia in 1858.

Large language models are neural networks trained on vast amounts of text to predict the next word, from which they learn to answer questions, summarise, translate and write code. The transformer architecture, published by Google researchers in 2017, made such training efficient on parallel hardware. From about 2020 very large models showed broad abilities, though they can state errors fluently.

A laser amplifies light by stimulated emission, which Albert Einstein described in 1917. Charles Townes's group built a microwave maser in the early 1950s; Townes and Arthur Schawlow patented an optical maser in 1958, a priority Gordon Gould contested. On 16 May 1960 Theodore Maiman operated the first laser, a synthetic ruby emitting red pulses, at Hughes Research Laboratories.

The lateen is a triangular fore-and-aft sail on a long, angled yard, letting a ship work closer to the wind than a square sail. A second-century CE gravestone appears to show a related four-sided form, and a wreck of about 400 CE is reconstructed with a lateen rig. Its origin is debated. It became typical of Arab and Mediterranean craft.

Latitude sailing finds a ship's north-south position from the height of the Sun at noon or of known stars, then holds it across open water. Settlers of remote Pacific islands from about 1,000 BCE are thought to have used star paths without instruments, while Greek astronomers by about 300 BCE linked latitude to day length. The traditions arose independently.

Written law sets rules and penalties down in a public text, so judges can apply a fixed wording rather than remembered custom alone. Among the earliest surviving collections are the laws of Ur-Namma of Ur, about 2100 BCE, and of Hammurabi of Babylon, about 1750 BCE, whose stele is in the Louvre. How closely courts followed such texts is debated.

The law of nations is a body of norms held to bind sovereign states in their dealings: the safety of envoys, the keeping of treaties, the rights of neutrals and limits on war. Hugo Grotius's On the Law of War and Peace (1625) systematised earlier natural-law writing. Lacking a common enforcer, it relied on custom, reciprocity and reputation.

Laws of war conventions are agreements by which states bind their conduct in armed conflict. The Lieber Code of 1863 instructed Union armies in the American Civil War; the Geneva Convention of 1864 protected wounded soldiers and medical staff; the Hague Conventions of 1899 addressed prisoners, occupation and some weapons. Compliance depended on reciprocity and command discipline; violations remained common.

Systematic law organizes legal rules into a reasoned whole, with general principles, categories of persons, property and obligations, and trained jurists who interpret and teach it. Roman jurists developed this approach, later compiled in Justinian's Corpus Juris Civilis of 529-534 CE. Comparable traditions include Islamic jurisprudence and the Chinese statutory codes, such as the Tang code of the seventh century.

Pulses were domesticated alongside cereals. Lentil, pea, chickpea and bitter vetch belong to Southwest Asia's founder crops of about 11,000 to 10,000 years ago, and the common bean was domesticated separately in Mesoamerica and the Andes from about 8,000 years ago. Rich in protein, legumes also host root bacteria that fix atmospheric nitrogen, renewing soil fertility.

Light-water reactors use ordinary water both to cool the core and to slow neutrons. Because water captures more neutrons than graphite or heavy water, their fuel is enriched to roughly 3-5% uranium-235. Pressurised designs came from the US naval programme, which also built Shippingport in 1957; boiling-water designs grew from Idaho's BORAX tests, which lit Arco in 1955.

Lime plaster is made by burning limestone into quicklime, slaking it with water and applying the paste, which hardens as it reabsorbs carbon dioxide from the air. Late Natufian graves at Nahal Ein Gev II, Israel, about 12,000 years old, were lined with it. Later Neolithic villagers laid polished plaster floors and modelled the statues of 'Ain Ghazal, Jordan.

A lithium-ion battery stores energy by moving lithium ions between two host materials that take them into their crystal layers. John Goodenough's group proposed a lithium cobalt oxide cathode in 1980, Akira Yoshino built a safer cell with a carbon anode in 1985, and commercial sales began in 1991. These light, rechargeable cells suited portable electronics and later electric vehicles.

A steam locomotive puts a high-pressure engine on wheels so that it can haul trains along rails. Richard Trevithick's engine pulled loaded wagons on the Penydarren tramroad in Wales in 1804. At the Rainhill trials of 1829, George and Robert Stephenson's Rocket, with a multi-tube boiler and steam blast, showed locomotives could run fast and reliably.

The longbow is a tall self bow, often of yew, about the archer's height, with a heavy draw. English armies of the fourteenth and fifteenth centuries combined massed archers with dismounted men-at-arms, as at Crécy in 1346. Its power came less from new technique than from years of practice; bows from the Mary Rose, sunk 1545, show their size.

Longitude by chronometer compares local noon with the time kept by an accurate clock set to a reference meridian; each hour of difference equals 15 degrees. Pendulum clocks failed at sea. John Harrison's marine timekeeper H4 erred by only seconds on a 1761-62 trial voyage to Jamaica. Chronometers became common on ships during the 19th century.

The warp-weighted loom hangs vertical warp threads from a beam, kept taut by bunches of clay or stone weights; the weaver stands and beats each weft upward. Rows of fallen loom weights mark looms at Anatolian and European sites from about the sixth millennium BCE. It wove wide cloth, including sailcloth, and survived in Norway into the twentieth century.

In lost-wax casting a model is made in wax, covered in clay and heated so the wax melts out, leaving a cavity for molten metal; the mould is broken, so each casting is unique. A copper amulet from Mehrgarh, Pakistan, about 6,000 years old, is the earliest known example, and the Nahal Mishmar hoard shows elaborate Chalcolithic work.

Crewed lunar flight required leaving Earth orbit, crossing roughly 384,000 kilometres, landing, and surviving a very fast re-entry. NASA's Apollo 8 orbited the Moon in December 1968, and in July 1969 Apollo 11's Neil Armstrong and Buzz Aldrin walked on its surface. Six Apollo missions landed between 1969 and 1972, returning about 382 kilograms of lunar samples.

Macadam roads, named after the Scottish engineer John Loudon McAdam, were built from layers of small, angular broken stone over a drained, cambered base, which traffic compacted into a hard, smooth surface. Adopted widely by British turnpike trusts from the 1820s, the method was cheaper than heavy paving and spread across Europe and North America.

Machine guns fire continuously while the trigger is held. Richard Gatling patented a hand-cranked gun with a rotating cluster of barrels in 1862. Hiram Maxim's gun, developed from about 1884, was fully automatic: recoil energy ejected each spent case and loaded the next round. In the First World War, machine guns, wire and artillery helped produce trench deadlock.

Machine learning builds programs that improve by fitting models to examples rather than following hand-written rules. Its roots include statistics and early learning machines such as the perceptron of the late 1950s. Backpropagation, popularised in 1986 by David Rumelhart, Geoffrey Hinton and Ronald Williams, trained networks with hidden layers, while decision trees and support-vector machines developed alongside.

Maize descends from teosinte, a wild grass of southwestern Mexico whose small ears hold kernels in hard, indigestible cases. Evidence from the Central Balsas River valley, where the closest wild relative still grows, places early domesticated maize about 8,700 years ago. Farmers gradually selected larger cobs whose softer-cased kernels stay attached, and maize spread north and south.

A Marxist-Leninist state is ruled by a communist party claiming to lead the working class, combining one-party rule with state ownership and planning. The Soviet Union, founded in 1922, was the first such state; the People's Republic of China followed in 1949. The USSR industrialised rapidly while suppressing opposition, then dissolved in 1991; China remains under communist rule.

A mass political party is a permanent organisation with local branches, a press and national leadership, built to mobilise voters. In the United States, national party organisations and nominating conventions formed around 1830. Germany's socialist party, created by a merger at Gotha in 1875, became a model of membership organisation. Parties widen participation but can concentrate power in leaderships.

Mass suffrage extends the vote to most adults, typically through public registers of electors and, increasingly, a secret ballot. Most US states dropped property qualifications for white men by about 1830; France adopted universal male suffrage in 1848; New Zealand gave women the national vote in 1893. Broad franchises long excluded many people by race, sex, residence or literacy.

The matchlock was the first mechanical firing lock: a curved lever, the serpentine, lowers a smouldering cord into a pan of priming powder, so the shooter can keep aiming while firing. Matchlock arquebuses spread in Europe in the later fifteenth century, using granulated, or corned, powder. Portuguese traders brought them to Japan in 1543, where smiths soon produced copies.

Archimedes of Syracuse, about 287-212 BCE, treated weights and floating bodies with geometric proof. In On the Equilibrium of Planes he proved the law of the lever and located centres of gravity; On Floating Bodies states that an immersed body is pushed up by a force equal to the weight of fluid displaced. He died when Rome took Syracuse.

Isaac Newton's Principia (1687) set out three laws of motion and a law of universal gravitation, and used them to derive Kepler's planetary laws mathematically. A single set of principles now covered falling bodies, projectiles and orbits, giving engineers and astronomers a shared method of calculation, though Newton declined to propose a cause for gravity.

Engines began replacing draught animals. John Froelich's petrol tractor worked Iowa's 1892 threshing season; Benjamin Holt tested a tracked steam tractor on Californian peat in 1904. Mass-produced Fordsons followed from 1917, and combines reaped and threshed in one pass. Machinery helped shrink US farm work from over a third of workers in 1900 to under 2 percent by 2000.

Cross-sectional imaging shows slices through the body instead of overlapping shadows. Godfrey Hounsfield's computed tomography scanner, which rotated an X-ray source and detectors and rebuilt the image by computer, scanned its first patient in London in 1971. Magnetic resonance imaging uses strong magnetic fields and radio waves, not ionising radiation, and produced its first human body scan in 1977.

Clinical medicine treats illness as a natural process to be observed at the bedside, recorded and reasoned about, not only as divine action. Several traditions systematised it in the first millennium BCE: the Hippocratic writings of Greece, from about 430 BCE; Ayurvedic compendia attributed to Charaka and Sushruta in India; and China's Inner Canon of the Yellow Emperor.

Medical texts fixed treatments in writing, so remedies could be copied and taught beyond one healer's memory. A Sumerian clay tablet from Nippur, of about 2100 BCE, lists prescriptions. The Egyptian Edwin Smith papyrus, copied about 1600 BCE from older material, sets out 48 injury cases in order: examination, diagnosis, a verdict on treatability, then treatment.

Gerardus Mercator's world map of 1569 used a projection that keeps angles true, so a line of constant compass bearing, a rhumb line, appears straight. Navigators could lay a course with a ruler. The price is exaggerated area toward the poles. Edward Wright published the mathematics for constructing the projection accurately in 1599.

A mercantile republic is governed by councils drawn from merchant families: a great council elects smaller councils and a closely limited head of state, and policy favours long-distance trade. Venice is the best-known case; from 1297 its Great Council was gradually closed to all but established families. Genoa, governed by consuls from about 1100, and Hanseatic Lübeck were comparable.

Writing arose in Mesoamerica independently of the Old World. Candidate early signs include a cylinder seal from San Andrés, Tabasco, of about 650 BCE, which its excavators read as writing though critics doubt it, and inscriptions from Oaxaca of about 400 BCE. Maya writing is attested at San Bartolo, Guatemala, by about 300 to 200 BCE.

Metallography studies the inner structure of metals. From 1863 to 1865 Henry Clifton Sorby of Sheffield polished and etched steel and examined it under reflected-light microscopes, revealing distinct constituents, including one he called 'pearly'. By about 1900 Roberts-Austen and Bakhuis Roozeboom had drawn the iron-carbon phase diagram; austenite, a high-temperature form of steel, is named after Roberts-Austen.

Microliths are small segments of blades or bladelets, often blunted along one edge, set in rows or at angles into wooden or bone shafts. In southern Africa's Howiesons Poort, about 65,000-60,000 years ago, backed quartz segments were hafted with ochre-and-gum glues, probably as arrow tips. Much later, Mesolithic Europeans used similar inserts as replaceable barbs and cutting edges.

A microprocessor places a computer's entire central processing unit on one chip. Intel's 4004, released in 1971 for a Japanese calculator maker, held about 2,300 transistors and handled four bits at a time. Cheap processors soon controlled instruments, appliances and vehicles, and made small general-purpose computers affordable. Other firms developed comparable chips at about the same time.

Dutch spectacle makers combined lenses in a tube around 1600, and the name microscope was coined in 1625. Robert Hooke's Micrographia (1665) described the 'cells' of cork. Antoni van Leeuwenhoek's tiny single lenses, magnifying up to about 270 times, revealed microorganisms, which he described in letters to the Royal Society from the 1670s.

Under military rule the armed forces, through their commanders or a council of officers, hold supreme power, govern by decree and subordinate or suspend civilian institutions, and rulers depend on the army's backing. Historical forms vary widely, including Japan's Kamakura shogunate from the 1180s-1190s, the Mamluk sultanate of Egypt and Syria (1250-1517), and many twentieth-century juntas.

Milking yields food repeatedly without killing the animal. Fat residues in more than 2,200 pottery vessels show milk in use by the seventh millennium BCE in the Near East and southeastern Europe, especially in northwestern Anatolia where cattle were common. The residues point mostly to processed foods such as butter, yogurt or cheese rather than fresh milk.

Broomcorn and foxtail millet, grasses that tolerate drought and short growing seasons, were the founding grains of farming in northern China. At Cishan in Hebei, a 2009 study dated domesticated broomcorn millet to about 10,000 years ago, although some archaeologists question its sampling and dates. Where and when each millet was first domesticated remains open.

A milling machine removes metal with a rotating, many-toothed cutter while the work is fed past it, shaping flat faces, slots and gear teeth more uniformly than hand filing. Early versions appeared in American arms works around 1816 to 1820, associated with Simeon North and with Eli Whitney's armory, though attribution is debated. Universal milling machines followed in the 1860s.

Systematic mineralogy sorts minerals into species by properties and, later, chemistry. Georgius Agricola, a physician in the Bohemian mining town Joachimsthal, classified minerals by physical properties in 1546. In 1758 Axel Fredrik Cronstedt proposed a mineral system, analysing specimens with a blowpipe flame. Such chemistry let Klaproth find uranium in 1789 in pitchblende, which miners had called bad luck.

Shaft mining follows good rock underground through vertical shafts and side galleries instead of digging only at the surface. Neolithic miners at Spiennes, Belgium, sank shafts up to 16 metres deep for flint from the late fifth millennium BCE. At the Great Orme in Wales, Bronze Age miners worked copper ore underground mainly between about 1600 and 1200 BCE.

Ministerial responsibility is the convention that ministers hold office only while they keep the confidence of the elected chamber. The collapse of Lord North's ministry in 1782, when George III had to accept ministers he opposed, is often cited as an early British marker. Nova Scotia won responsible government in 1848. It makes executives accountable but can destabilise fragile governments.

Missile defence tries to detect, track and destroy attacking missiles before they reach their targets. The 1972 Anti-Ballistic Missile Treaty limited American and Soviet systems, which then relied on nuclear-armed interceptors. In June 1984 an American test, the Homing Overlay Experiment, destroyed a target warhead by direct collision, the hit-to-kill approach later used by several systems.

Cellular telephony divides an area into cells, each served by a low-power radio base station, so frequencies can be reused and calls handed between stations as users move. Bell Labs engineers proposed the idea in 1947. The first commercial automatic cellular network opened in Tokyo in 1979, followed by Nordic NMT in 1981 and American AMPS in 1983.

Monoclonal antibodies are identical antibodies made by a single cloned cell line, all binding one chosen target. In 1975 Georges Köhler and César Milstein in Cambridge fused antibody-producing cells with myeloma cells, creating immortal 'hybridoma' lines. Engineered versions became precise diagnostic reagents and, from the late 1980s and 1990s, medicines against cancers and autoimmune diseases.

Monsoon navigation times voyages to the Indian Ocean's seasonal winds, which blow from the southwest in summer and the northeast in winter. Greek and Roman sources describe ships crossing directly from Arabia or the Red Sea to India by about the 1st century BCE, though Arabian and Indian sailors probably used the pattern earlier. Departures followed the seasons.

In mortise-and-tenon construction, shipwrights cut slots in adjoining hull planks and lock them with tight tongues pinned by pegs, building the shell before inserting frames. The Uluburun wreck off southern Turkey, about 1,300 BCE, carried copper, tin and glass in such a hull. Roman builders used the method for large grain ships linking Egypt to Rome.

A motor road, or highway, is built for fast motor traffic alone, with limited access points and few or no level crossings. Italy's Milano-Laghi autostrada, opened in 1924, was a tolled road reserved for motor vehicles; Germany's Cologne-Bonn road of 1932 is often cited as an early crossing-free, dual-carriageway motorway. Such roads made trucking a major channel for long-distance freight.

According to the scholar Shen Kuo, in the 1040s a commoner named Bi Sheng made individual characters from baked clay, set them in an iron frame bedded in wax and resin, and printed pages before softening the bedding to reuse the type. No example survives. Because Chinese uses thousands of characters, woodblocks remained dominant for centuries.

Korea's Goryeo kingdom printed with cast metal type by the thirteenth century; a written record describes a ritual text printed this way around 1234, though no copy survives. The Jikji, a Buddhist anthology printed in 1377 at Heungdeok temple, is the oldest extant book printed with movable metal type. Later Joseon state foundries cast large type sets.

An mRNA vaccine delivers genetic instructions, packaged in lipid nanoparticles, so that the body's own cells make a viral protein and prime the immune system. It drew on decades of work, including chemically modified nucleosides that reduce unwanted inflammation (Karikó and Weissman, 2005). After the SARS-CoV-2 genome was published in January 2020, authorised vaccines were in use by that December.

Mudbrick is earth mixed with water and often straw or dung, shaped by hand or in moulds and dried in the sun. Hand-shaped bricks were used at Jericho by roughly 9,000 BCE, and Çatalhöyük in Anatolia was a dense mudbrick town by about 7,000 BCE. Cheap and insulating, mudbrick needs regular replastering; repeated rebuilding slowly raises settlement mounds.

A municipal charter is a written grant by which a ruler lets a town govern itself, with its own council, magistrates, courts and market, for loyalty and fixed payments. Bronze tablets of the Lex Irnitana, a town law from Flavian Roman Spain of the late first century CE, survive, and many European towns obtained charters from the eleventh and twelfth centuries.

Nanoscale engineering works with structures roughly 1 to 100 nanometres across, where surface and quantum effects change how materials behave. The scanning tunnelling microscope, built at IBM Zurich in 1981, made single atoms visible; in 1989 IBM researchers moved xenon atoms to spell the company's initials. Fullerenes (1985) and carbon nanotubes (1991) followed as new carbon forms.

From around the eighth century BCE, Mediterranean war galleys carried a bronze-sheathed ram at the waterline, turning the oared ship itself into a weapon. The trireme, with three tiers of rowers, became the leading type by the late sixth century BCE. The Athlit ram, found off Israel and dated to about the second century BCE, survives intact.

After 1492, ocean contact moved crops between the hemispheres. Maize, potatoes, sweet potatoes and cassava spread across Europe, Asia and Africa; one economic study attributes about a quarter of Old World population growth between 1700 and 1900 to the potato. In the Americas, Old World crops and livestock spread, and sugar and coffee plantations relied on enslaved labour.

Nixtamalization means cooking and soaking maize in an alkaline solution of lime, wood ash or crushed shell. It loosens the hulls, eases grinding into dough, and releases bound niacin, protecting people who live mostly on maize from pellagra. The earliest suggested evidence, cooking equipment on Guatemala's southern coast, dates to about 1500 to 1200 BCE.

Water-lifting wheels raise water above a river or canal to fields beyond gravity's reach. The saqiya, an animal-driven geared wheel carrying a chain of pots, is attested in Ptolemaic Egypt by about the third century BCE. Wheels turned by the current, later called norias, were described by Roman writers; large medieval-origin examples still stand at Hama, Syria.

A controlled chain reaction keeps uranium fission steady: each splitting nucleus releases two or three neutrons, and on average one causes the next fission. A moderator such as very pure graphite slows the neutrons; absorbing rods set the pace. The first such pile, CP-1, ran on 2 December 1942 beneath a Chicago stadium's stands, producing about half a watt.

Controlled fusion research tries to join light nuclei such as deuterium and tritium in a plasma hot, dense and confined enough to yield net energy. Soviet physicists developed the tokamak, a doughnut-shaped magnetic chamber, in the 1950s. Inertial confinement squeezes fuel pellets with lasers; a 2022 American experiment released more energy than its lasers delivered.

Nuclear medicine places radioactive substances in the body to trace organ function or treat disease. George de Hevesy's tracer method, first published in 1923, used radioactive atoms to mark an element's path. In 1941 Saul Hertz in Boston treated thyroid disease with radioiodine. Technetium-99m generators, first ordered by a hospital in 1961, now serve some 40 million procedures yearly.

Nuclear physics studies the atom's tiny, dense nucleus, identified by Ernest Rutherford in 1911. Isotopes, the neutron (James Chadwick, 1932) and artificial radioactivity (1934) followed. In December 1938 Otto Hahn and Fritz Strassmann found barium among products of neutron-irradiated uranium; Lise Meitner and Otto Frisch explained it as nuclear splitting, and Niels Bohr traced slow-neutron fission to uranium-235.

A nuclear power station uses reactor heat to raise steam for turbines, and its engineering spans grid and core. Obninsk in the Soviet Union sent about 5 megawatts to the grid in June 1954; Calder Hall in England and Shippingport in the United States followed in 1956-57. Operators plan refuelling outages, size units to the grid and protect cooling power.

A nuclear submarine is driven by a compact reactor that makes steam for its turbines, so propulsion needs no air and the boat can stay submerged far longer than diesel-electric craft. The US Navy's Nautilus, powered by a pressurised-water reactor from Hyman Rickover's naval programme, signalled 'underway on nuclear power' on 17 January 1955. Other navies followed.

In base-60 place value, one wedge sign can mean 1, 60 or 3,600 by its position, so one set of rules serves multiplication, division and fractions. Mesopotamian scribes adopted it for calculation probably in the Ur III period, about 2100-2000 BCE, converting their measures into it. Lacking a zero sign or point, readers judged magnitude from context.

Numerical control directs a machine tool by coded instructions instead of a machinist's hands. John Parsons proposed the idea for cutting aircraft parts, and MIT's Servomechanisms Laboratory demonstrated a tape-controlled milling machine in 1952. In 1961 the Unimate, a programmable arm designed by George Devol and promoted by Joseph Engelberger, began handling hot die-castings at a General Motors plant.

Before writing, separate villages or kin groups could bind themselves together through public oaths, exchanges of gifts and marriages between their families, calling down divine or communal sanctions on anyone who broke faith. Such alliances are known from ethnography and inferred for prehistory. The earliest written examples, from Ebla in Syria around 2400 BCE, already record oaths sworn before gods.

The ocean-going junk combined a compartmented hull, a large rudder and battened sails with compass navigation, recorded at sea in 1111-1117. Song and Yuan merchants sailed such ships between China, Southeast Asia and India with the monsoons. The Quanzhou wreck of about 1275 had thirteen compartments, and Zheng He's fleets reached East Africa between 1405 and 1433.

Ochres are iron-rich earths that grind into red or yellow pigment. At Blombos Cave, South Africa, people about 100,000 years ago rubbed ochre on quartzite slabs into powder, mixed it with other ingredients and stored the liquid in two abalone shells, beside grindstones and bone tools. Its purpose, decoration, skin protection or something else, remains unknown.

A statistical office is a standing public body that collects and publishes counts at regular intervals, turning single censuses into comparable series. Sweden's Tabellverket compiled national population tables from parish registers from 1749. Britain took its first national census in 1801. Regular tables let governments track births, deaths and migration, though their categories reflected official priorities.

Olive oil is made by crushing the fruit to a paste and pressing it to separate oil from water and pulp. Residues in pottery from En Zippori in Galilee show olive oil in use about 5800 BCE, and underwater remains off Kfar Samir, near Haifa, preserve an early processing site. Oil served as food and lamp fuel, and stored well.

The beam press squeezes crushed olives with a long wooden lever: one end is anchored in a wall socket and the other is pulled down by heavy stones, multiplying the force on baskets of pulp below. At Tel Miqne-Ekron, a Philistine city, more than a hundred such installations produced oil for export in the seventh century BCE.

A one-party state allows only one legal political party, or tolerates others only under its control, and merges party and state offices. In Soviet Russia the communist party held a monopoly of power from soon after 1917; the Republican People's Party governed Turkey alone from about 1925 to 1945. Such regimes have pursued very different ideologies.

Open-hearth steelmaking melted pig iron with scrap and ore in a shallow hearth heated by Carl Wilhelm Siemens's regenerative furnace, which used waste heat to preheat gas and air. Pierre-Émile Martin first made steel this way at Sireuil, France, in 1864-65. Slower than a converter, it let steelmakers sample and adjust each charge, and it consumed scrap.

An operating system is the software that manages a computer's processor, memory, storage and devices, sharing them among programs and users. Time-sharing systems of the 1960s, such as CTSS and Multics at MIT, let many users work at once. Unix, begun at Bell Labs in 1969 and largely rewritten in the C language by 1973, could be moved between machines.

In July 1794 the engineer Claude Chappe, helped by his brothers, completed a line of fifteen signal stations between Paris and Lille. Operators set movable arms into coded positions that the next station, 10 to 15 kilometres away, read by telescope and repeated. The French network spanned nearly 5,000 kilometres. Sweden and Britain built shutter systems from 1795.

Ibn al-Haytham's Book of Optics, written in Cairo between about 1010 and 1021, argued that we see because light reflected from objects enters the eye, rejecting the older idea of rays sent out from the eye. He supported claims with controlled set-ups, such as light admitted through a small hole into a darkened chamber. Latin translations later shaped European optics.

Oral rehydration therapy treats the dehydration of diarrhoeal diseases such as cholera with a drink of clean water, salts and glucose. Glucose helps the gut absorb sodium, and water follows, even during infection. Trials in Dhaka and Calcutta in the late 1960s showed that it worked, and during the 1971 Bangladesh refugee crisis it sharply reduced cholera deaths.

An orbital launch vehicle is a staged, guided rocket able to reach orbital speed, about 7.8 kilometres per second at low altitude. Earlier missiles such as the German V-2 (1944) reached only a fraction of that speed. The Soviet R-7, built as an intercontinental missile, first flew full range in August 1957 and launched Sputnik 1 on 4 October.

Fruit trees take years to bear and are often propagated from cuttings rather than seed. Carbonised seedless figs from Gilgal near Jericho, about 11,400 years old, could only have spread through planted shoots, suggesting very early fig cultivation. Olives, grapes and dates were domesticated thousands of years later; olive oil residues in Galilee pottery date to about 5800 BCE.

Ore prospecting means reading the ground for metal-bearing rock: green and blue copper stains, rusty weathered caps called gossans, and heavy dark pebbles in stream gravels that may be tin ore. At Rudna Glava in Serbia, Vinča-culture miners followed copper veins by the fifth millennium BCE. Tin ore was scarcer and harder to recognise; its earliest sources are debated.

Organ transplantation replaces a failing organ with one from a donor. In Boston in 1954, Joseph Murray's team transplanted a kidney between identical twins, avoiding immune rejection. Transplants between unrelated people needed drugs to suppress rejection: azathioprine in the early 1960s, then cyclosporine, approved in the early 1980s, which greatly improved survival of kidney, liver and heart grafts.

Organic chemistry studies the compounds of carbon. In 1828 Friedrich Wöhler made urea, an organic compound, from inorganic starting materials, weakening the belief that such compounds need a vital force, although the effect was gradual. From 1858 structural theory showed which atoms bond to which, and August Kekulé proposed the ring structure of benzene in 1865.

An organized priesthood is a body of full-time religious specialists who serve a temple, keep its festival calendar and manage its lands, herds and offerings. At Eridu in southern Mesopotamia a long sequence of superimposed temples begins in the Ubaid period, perhaps about 5500 BCE, and by about 3300-3000 BCE tablets at Uruk recorded goods and workers' rations.

Paper is a mat of plant fibres beaten to pulp, caught on a screen and dried. Fragments from Han China, including a map-bearing piece from Fangmatan, are dated to the second century BCE. The official Cai Lun is credited with improving the craft in 105 CE. Papermaking reached Central Asia and Baghdad by the eighth century, and Europe later.

Merchants in Sichuan issued paper deposit receipts called jiaozi around the year 1000, partly because local iron coins were heavy. In the 1020s the Song state took over their issue, creating the first government paper currency, printed from blocks. Later issues, notably under the Yuan, were overprinted, and inflation repeatedly eroded confidence in the notes.

Papyrus sheets were made by laying thin strips of the papyrus sedge's pith in two crossed layers, then pressing and drying them into a smooth surface. A blank roll found in the First Dynasty tomb of Hemaka at Saqqara shows the material in use by about 3000 BCE. Egypt supplied papyrus rolls to Greek and Roman writers for many centuries.

Parliamentary government is rule by a cabinet drawn from and responsible to the legislature, governing only while it keeps a majority's confidence. In Britain, after the 1832 Reform Act no cabinet could survive without a Commons majority, and by the mid-1800s the cabinet was the senior decision-making body. Fused executives can legislate quickly but fall when majorities break.

A patent is a temporary exclusive right that a state grants an inventor for a new device or process, in exchange for disclosing it, under a set legal procedure. Venice passed a general patent statute in 1474; England's 1624 Statute of Monopolies curbed royal monopolies but kept invention patents; France and the United States enacted patent laws in 1790-1791.

Pattern welding forge-welds bars or rods of iron and steel, often twisted, into one blade; grinding reveals wavy or chevron patterns. Occasional twisted strips appear in late La Tene swords; the true technique is evident from about the third century CE, reached its greatest complexity in the sixth and seventh centuries, and had largely ended by the late tenth.

The polymerase chain reaction copies a chosen stretch of DNA again and again by repeatedly heating and cooling a sample with short primers and a DNA-copying enzyme. Kary Mullis devised it at the Cetus Corporation in 1983 and shared the 1993 Nobel Prize in Chemistry. A heat-stable enzyme from the bacterium Thermus aquaticus made the cycles practical.

Percussion drilling repeatedly lifts and drops a heavy iron bit, chipping a narrow hole downward. Sichuan drillers used it to reach brine and natural gas; around 1050 CE, in the Song dynasty, a light, flexible bamboo cable replaced heavy solid bamboo rods. Zigong's Shenhai well passed about 1,001 metres in 1835. Pennsylvania's 1859 Drake oil well used a cable-tool rig.

In 1869 Dmitri Mendeleev arranged the known elements by atomic weight so that similar properties recurred at regular intervals, leaving gaps for undiscovered ones. He forecast the properties of 'eka-aluminium' and 'eka-silicon', matched by gallium (1875) and germanium (1886). Lothar Meyer published a comparable periodic table in 1870 but was more reluctant to predict new elements.

A personal computer is cheap and small enough for one person to own and use. Microcomputer kits appeared in 1974-75, and in 1977 the Apple II, Commodore PET and TRS-80 were sold ready-built to homes, schools and offices. Programs such as the VisiCalc spreadsheet of 1979 made them business tools, and IBM's PC of 1981 widened adoption.

Crude oil is a mixture of hydrocarbons that boil at different temperatures, so heating separates lighter and heavier fractions. In Lviv in the early 1850s the pharmacists Ignacy Łukasiewicz and Jan Zeh distilled lamp oil (kerosene); a kerosene lamp lit a hospital operation there in 1853. Łukasiewicz opened a refinery in 1856, three years before Edwin Drake's Pennsylvania well.

A pharmacopoeia is a systematic catalogue of medicinal substances: what each is, where it comes from, how it is prepared and what it treats. The Greek physician Dioscorides compiled De materia medica in the first century CE, describing about 600 plants, and it was copied for some fifteen centuries. China's Shennong herbal classic and Indian compendia built comparable traditions.

Photography fixes the image formed by a lens with light-sensitive silver compounds. Louis Daguerre's process, announced in Paris in 1839, gave a single sharp image on a silvered copper plate. William Henry Fox Talbot showed his own paper process the same year; his calotype, patented in 1841, produced a negative from which many positive prints could be made.

Physiology studies how the body's parts work, not only their form. William Harvey's De motu cordis (1628) used ligature experiments and estimates of how much blood the heart pumps to show that blood circulates continuously. Ibn al-Nafis had described the blood's passage through the lungs in the thirteenth century. Marcello Malpighi described the capillaries closing Harvey's circuit in 1661.

Pigs descend from wild boar and were domesticated independently in southwestern Asia and in China, roughly by 8,500 BCE and 6,000 BCE respectively. Genetic studies show that Europe's first domestic pigs came from the Near East, and suggest further local domestications in South and Southeast Asia. Pigs need no pasture: they eat scraps and forage, and breed quickly.

A plank-built boat assembles a hull from shaped boards, sewn with cord or fastened with pegs, instead of carving it from one log, so hull size is no longer limited by a single tree. Copper and bronze tools eased the joinery. Khufu's ship at Giza, about 2,500 BCE, and the sewn-plank Ferriby boats from England's Humber show separate traditions.

Synthetic polymers are long chain molecules built from small repeating units. Leo Baekeland's Bakelite, made from phenol and formaldehyde and introduced around 1907-1909, was the first fully synthetic plastic and set hard when heated. In the 1930s polyethylene was made at ICI in Britain and nylon at DuPont, first sold as toothbrush bristles (1938) and stockings (1939).

Plate armour covers the body with shaped, hardened iron or steel plates articulated at the joints. European armourers moved from mail reinforced with plates to complete plate harness during the fourteenth century; by the early fifteenth, full harness was usual for wealthy men-at-arms. Quenching and tempering made plates hard but not brittle. A harness typically weighed 15 to 25 kilograms.

An ard is a simple plough: a pointed share dragged through the soil by animals, scratching a furrow without turning it over, so fields were often cross-ploughed. The oldest known plough marks in Europe, at Sion in Switzerland, date to the early fifth millennium BCE. By the fourth millennium BCE ploughing with draught animals is attested in Europe and Mesopotamia.

Polynesian voyaging canoes joined two hulls, or one hull and an outrigger, under woven sails, carrying people, plants and animals across thousands of kilometres of ocean. Navigators steered by stars, swells and birds without compass or writing. Hawaii was reached by around 1000-1200 CE and New Zealand by about 1300, late steps in a much older settlement of Oceania.

Portland cement is made by burning limestone or chalk with clay into clinker and grinding it to a powder that hardens with water. Joseph Aspdin patented the name in 1824, after Portland stone, but his product was probably underburned. Firing at much higher temperatures, as Isaac Charles Johnson did around 1845-50, produced the stronger modern material.

A portolan chart draws coastlines from compass bearings and estimated sailing distances, criss-crossed by radiating lines that help a navigator lay a course. The oldest surviving example, the Carte Pisane, dates from the late 13th century and covers the Mediterranean and Black Sea. Its makers drew on sailors' observations, not on Ptolemy's coordinate grid.

A fast wheel spins with enough momentum to keep turning between pushes, so a potter can raise a vessel from a centred lump of clay. In Mesopotamia it was adopted in the fourth millennium BCE within the Uruk world and spread unevenly. The mass-produced bevelled-rim bowls of that era, however, were probably shaped in moulds, not thrown on a wheel.

Shaping clay into vessels and firing them in an open bonfire produces porous but heat-resistant containers for boiling and storage. Pottery arose separately in several regions: sherds from Xianrendong Cave, China, date to about 20,000 years ago, and Odai Yamamoto in Japan to about 16,500 years ago. African and Near Eastern pottery traditions began later and independently.

A power loom performs weaving's repeated motions by machine: raising warp threads, throwing the shuttle across, and beating in the weft. It mechanised John Kay's flying shuttle (1733). Edmund Cartwright patented early designs from 1785, but practical looms needed later improvements by others. By about 1820 steam looms were spreading in Britain; Waltham, Massachusetts, wove by water power from 1814.

Precision agriculture treats a field as a patchwork rather than a uniform unit. In the early 1990s, yield monitors on combines logged grain flow against satellite positions, and the maps showed yields varying within fields. Variable-rate machines, adopted from the late 1990s, adjusted seed and fertiliser by location. Uptake was uneven: early returns were inconsistent and data standards lagged.

A presidential republic has a chief executive elected separately from the legislature for a fixed term, who cannot normally be removed by a vote of no confidence. The United States Constitution of 1787 established the model, later adopted widely in Latin America and elsewhere. Fixed terms give predictability, though conflict between president and legislature can bring deadlock or constitutional crises.

Instead of striking, a knapper presses a pointed tool of bone, antler or wood against an edge to push off thin, controlled flakes. At Blombos Cave, South Africa, at least half the Still Bay points, made from about 76,000 years ago in heat-treated silcrete, were finished this way. Solutrean knappers in France and Spain later used pressure retouch too.

Around 1450 in Mainz, the metalworker Johannes Gutenberg combined a hand mould for casting uniform metal type, a lead-based type alloy, oil-based ink and a screw press adapted from presses used for wine and paper. His Bible appeared by about 1455. By 1500 presses had operated in more than two hundred European towns, sharply lowering the cost of books.

Probability became mathematics in 1654, when Blaise Pascal and Pierre de Fermat exchanged letters on dividing the stakes of an interrupted game. Jacob Bernoulli's Ars Conjectandi, published posthumously in 1713, proved that observed frequencies approach the underlying probability as trials multiply. Pierre-Simon Laplace's 1812 treatise built these ideas into general methods of calculation and inference.

The first programmable digital computers performed long calculations automatically, following instructions set by punched tape, switches or plugboard wiring rather than held in memory. They arose largely independently: Konrad Zuse's relay-based Z3 ran in Berlin in 1941; valve-based Colossus machines attacked German teleprinter ciphers at Bletchley Park from 1944; and ENIAC, completed in Philadelphia in 1945-46, computed artillery tables.

High-level programming languages let people write instructions in notation close to mathematics or English, which a compiler translates into machine code. FORTRAN, developed by John Backus's team at IBM and released in 1957, showed that compiled programs could run efficiently enough for scientific work. COBOL, LISP and ALGOL soon followed, making software easier to write and share.

The earliest clay tablets from Uruk in southern Mesopotamia, dated to about 3300-3000 BCE, record rations, livestock, land and labour using numerical signs and pictographic signs for goods and officials. Most are administrative accounts rather than written speech. Scribes used several different counting systems depending on what was counted, and the script only partly recorded language.

Provincial administration divides a realm into provinces, each under a governor sent by the centre to levy taxes and raise troops in the ruler's name, watched by officials and reports answering to the capital. Akkad placed governors over conquered cities around 2300 BCE; Assyria reorganized its provinces under Tiglath-Pileser III after 745 BCE; Persia's satrapies followed from about 520 BCE.

A board of health is a public authority empowered to protect a population's health through quarantine, inspection and sanitation. Ragusa, now Dubrovnik, ordered isolation of arrivals during plague in 1377, and Venice later kept a permanent health magistracy. England's General Board of Health, created in 1848, pressed for drains and clean water. They often acted before disease causes were understood.

Public-key cryptography uses a pair of keys: one can be published so anyone can encrypt messages or check signatures, while only its owner holds the other. Whitfield Diffie and Martin Hellman published the idea in 1976, and Rivest, Shamir and Adleman described the RSA system in 1977. British government cryptographers had found similar methods earlier, kept secret until 1997.

Puddling turned brittle pig iron into tough wrought iron without charcoal. In a coal-fired reverberatory furnace, where flame rather than fuel touched the metal, workers stirred molten iron until air burned out its carbon; the iron was then shingled and passed through grooved rolls. Henry Cort patented the rolls in 1783 and puddling in 1784; Welsh ironmasters made them practical.

Herman Hollerith, who had worked on the 1880 United States census, patented a system in 1889 that recorded each person as holes punched in a card. Electrical contacts through the holes advanced counters on a tabulating machine. Used for the 1890 census, it reportedly saved years of work. Hollerith's company later became part of IBM.

A qanat taps groundwater at the foot of hills and leads it through a gently sloping tunnel to fields and settlements downslope, without pumping. Diggers sink a line of vertical shafts for access, spoil removal and ventilation. Developed in Iran, probably during the first millennium BCE, qanats spread to North Africa, Spain and western China, and some still flow today.

A quantum computer stores information in qubits, which can hold superpositions and become entangled, so some calculations proceed in ways ordinary computers cannot efficiently imitate. Richard Feynman argued in 1981-82 that they could simulate physics. In 2019 Google's 53-qubit Sycamore processor ran a narrow sampling task claimed to be beyond classical reach, a claim IBM disputed. Early machines remain noisy.

Quantum mechanics describes matter and light at the atomic scale, where energy comes in discrete amounts. Max Planck introduced energy quanta in 1900, and Niels Bohr quantised atomic orbits in 1913. In 1925 Werner Heisenberg, Max Born and Pascual Jordan formulated matrix mechanics, and in 1926 Erwin Schrödinger published wave mechanics; the two proved mathematically equivalent.

Plunging red-hot carburized steel into water or another liquid traps carbon in a very hard but brittle crystal structure, now called martensite. A curved iron knife from an eleventh-century BCE tomb at Idalion, Cyprus, was analysed by the metallurgist Erik Tholander as quench-hardened steel, one of the earliest reported cases, though known here only from secondary accounts.

Radar detects distant objects by transmitting radio pulses and timing their echoes. It rests on the electromagnetic waves Heinrich Hertz demonstrated in the late 1880s. In the 1930s Britain, Germany, the United States and others developed it largely in parallel; Britain's Chain Home stations operated by the late 1930s. The cavity magnetron, from 1940, made compact microwave sets possible.

Radiation detectors make invisible ionising radiation measurable. Early workers counted alpha particles as flashes on zinc sulphide screens. Hans Geiger built an electrical counter in Rutherford's laboratory from 1908, developed with Walther Müller in 1928 into a tube sensitive to many kinds of radiation. Wilson's cloud chamber (1911) showed particle tracks; film badges and, from 1948, sodium-iodide scintillators extended measurement.

Radiation protection limits harm from ionising radiation by controlling time, distance, shielding and containment, and by measuring doses against agreed limits. Injuries to early X-ray workers and to radium dial painters who shaped brushes with their lips showed the danger. An international committee formed in Stockholm in 1928, later the ICRP; Chicago's wartime Metallurgical Laboratory named 'health physics' in 1942.

Heinrich Hertz demonstrated electromagnetic waves in 1886-1888. From 1895 Guglielmo Marconi built on Hertz's oscillator and Branly's coherer to send Morse code without wires, and in December 1901 he reported receiving a signal across the Atlantic in Newfoundland, a claim later questioned. Alexander Popov, Oliver Lodge and others did parallel work, and who invented radio remains disputed.

Voice radio needs continuous waves whose strength is varied, or modulated, by sound. Reginald Fessenden promoted amplitude modulation and reportedly broadcast speech and music from Brant Rock, Massachusetts, on Christmas Eve 1906. Pittsburgh's Westinghouse station KDKA made what is often called the first scheduled broadcast on 2 November 1920, though several stations claim to have been first.

Radioactivity is the spontaneous emission of radiation by unstable atoms. In 1896 Henri Becquerel found that uranium salts fogged wrapped photographic plates without sunlight. Marie and Pierre Curie, measuring tiny electric currents, identified polonium and radium in pitchblende in 1898. Rutherford and Frederick Soddy explained the rays as atoms transforming into other elements; handlers soon found radiation burns skin.

Radioisotopes can be made by bombarding stable atoms with particles. Irène Joliot-Curie and Frédéric Joliot made the first artificial radioactive isotope in 1934, and Ernest Lawrence's cyclotrons soon produced hundreds more. Reactors made isotopes plentiful: Oak Ridge sent its first, carbon-14, to a St Louis cancer hospital in August 1946. Cobalt-60 now sterilises medical devices, and iridium-192 serves industrial radiography.

Radiometric prospecting seeks uranium and thorium by detecting the gamma radiation around rocks rich in them. In the American uranium boom after the 1948 government price guarantee, Geological Survey teams drove roads with Geiger counters; airborne surveys were established by 1958. Modern spectrometers map potassium, uranium and thorium separately. About one exploration project in a thousand finds an economic deposit.

Radiotherapy uses radiation to destroy tumours while sparing healthy tissue. Soon after radium was seen to burn skin around 1901, doctors applied it to skin lesions, then placed sealed sources in body cavities or implanted needles. Centres such as the Paris radium institute developed the practice. From 1951 cobalt-60 units in London, Ontario, and Saskatoon delivered penetrating external beams.

A sea-crossing raft binds logs, bamboo or reed bundles into a platform buoyant enough to carry people over open water. No Pleistocene craft survives; such vessels are inferred from where people arrived. Settling Sahul, the joined landmass of Australia and New Guinea, required sea crossings by at least 50,000 years ago; the craft's form is unknown.

A railway network joins locomotives, iron rails, surveyed gradients, stations and timetables into a public system. The Liverpool and Manchester Railway, opened in 1830, was the first intercity line worked by steam locomotives and carrying passengers and freight to a timetable. Expanding networks cut inland freight costs, linked national markets and spread standardised railway time.

Mechanical refrigeration uses work to pump heat out of an insulated space, typically by compressing and evaporating a working fluid. In 1876 Carl von Linde, prompted by brewers, built a reliable ammonia compression machine; one served the Dreher brewery in Trieste for decades. In the same years refrigerated ships such as Ferdinand Carré's Paraguay began carrying frozen meat across oceans.

Reinforced concrete embeds iron or steel bars in concrete: the concrete resists crushing, the metal carries tension, and both expand similarly with heat. Joseph Monier, a Paris gardener, patented reinforced planters in 1867 and later wider uses; Joseph-Louis Lambot and William Wilkinson had experimented earlier. François Hennebique's 1892 system joined beams and columns into monolithic frames for buildings and bridges.

A relational database stores information as tables of rows and columns and retrieves it by stating what is wanted rather than how to find it. Edgar F. Codd of IBM set out the relational model in a 1970 paper. Research systems in the 1970s and commercial products around 1980 followed, and the SQL query language became the common standard.

Albert Einstein's special relativity (1905) held that light's speed is the same for all observers, so measured time and length depend on motion, and implied that mass and energy are equivalent. His general relativity (1915) described gravity as the curvature of spacetime. Satellite navigation clocks must be corrected for both effects, by about 38 microseconds a day.

Religious toleration lets communities of more than one faith worship openly and keep their own institutions without civil penalty for belonging to a minority. Ashoka's edicts in third-century BCE India urged respect between sects; the Edict of Milan in 313 CE allowed Christians to worship in the Roman empire; and France's Edict of Nantes, in 1598, granted Protestants limited rights.

A representative assembly summons spokesmen of the realm's estates or communities, typically nobles, clergy and towns, to consent to taxes and new laws and to petition for redress of grievances. At León in 1188, elected town representatives joined the royal council of Alfonso IX, and in 1265 Simon de Montfort's English parliament summoned borough burgesses alongside knights of the shires.

Reprocessing dissolves spent reactor fuel in nitric acid and separates uranium and plutonium from fission products by solvent extraction, the PUREX method. Wartime separation chemistry worked out at Oak Ridge's X-10 was used at Hanford to extract weapons plutonium. Civil plants such as France's La Hague, operating since 1976, recycle plutonium into mixed-oxide fuel. The United States runs none.

A resident embassy is a permanent mission at a foreign ruler's court whose ambassador reports home continuously. Venice, Milan and Mantua exchanged resident envoys from around 1400; such missions became normal in Italy late in the fifteenth century and spread northward after 1500. Earlier diplomacy relied mainly on temporary envoys. Standing missions gave steady information but invited suspicion of spying.

Reusable launch vehicles recover expensive hardware instead of discarding it. The US Space Shuttle (1981 to 2011) reused its orbiter and solid boosters but needed costly refurbishment between missions. In December 2015 SpaceX landed the first stage of a Falcon 9 orbital rocket upright after launch, using engine relights, grid fins and satellite navigation; reflights followed in 2017.

Early-ripening rice can be harvested after a shorter season, sometimes allowing two crops a year, and tolerates drought. After a drought on the lower Yangtze and Huai rivers in 1012, the Song emperor Zhenzong had seed of such rice, called Champa rice after its Southeast Asian source, sent from Fujian and distributed to farmers in the affected region.

At Kuahuqiao on the lower Yangtze, about 7,700 years ago, villagers burned scrub on a coastal swamp, kept fields wet and probably controlled flooding with low banks, an early form of paddy farming. The site was later drowned by the sea. Fully domesticated, non-shattering rice emerged in the region over the following thousand years or so.

Rifled breech-loading guns fired elongated shells that spun in flight, reaching farther and more accurately than round shot. William Armstrong's built-up gun, with coils shrunk over a rifled inner tube, entered British service in 1859, though Britain reverted to muzzle-loaders in the mid-1860s. Prussia adopted its first Krupp breech-loader, forged from solid steel, in 1856; Krupp persevered with the principle.

Rifling cuts spiral grooves inside a gun barrel so the projectile spins, flying straighter and farther. Rifled barrels were known in Europe by the fifteenth century, though who first made them is unclear. Because a tight ball had to be forced into the grooves, rifles loaded slowly; broad military use followed the Minié bullet, adopted about 1852.
